warmup.q: data class Cart(val id: String, val items: MutableList<String>). You run val c2 = c1.copy(id = "c2") and then c2.items += "milk". What happens to c1.items?
options: It now contains milk too, because both carts share one list
It throws, because data class properties can't change
It depends on whether c1 was declared with val
warmup.why: copy() is shallow. It copies the reference to the list, not the list, so c1 and c2 hold the same MutableList. val only stops you from pointing the property at another list; it says nothing about what's inside the list. Java records behave the same way. The last section of this lesson takes it apart and fixes it.

opening:
At the town's sandwich counter, nobody orders by reciting eight words in a fixed order. You say "rye bread", then "cheese", then "no onions", and the person behind the counter adds each part as you go. At the end they check that it really is a sandwich, with bread and a filling, and hand it over finished. Down the street, the print shop has a photocopier. Fill in a form once, copy it, change two lines on each copy, and you've saved an hour.

Objects with many optional parts have the same two needs. A constructor with seven parameters is a sandwich ordered in one breath, and nobody can tell which true meant "fragile". And a copy that changes two fields is so handy that it's easy to miss what it didn't copy.

In the last lesson, factories decided which class to make. In this lesson, we'll decide how to make one object with many parts: Kotlin's named and default arguments, a Java record with a builder, a Kotlin DSL for nested orders, and copies that never share what they shouldn't. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started at the sandwich counter and the photocopier. In code, named arguments let you order in one breath, and a builder still earns its place for Java callers and nested orders. Copies were the surprise: every copy() and wither shares whatever its fields point to.

Now look in your own code for a data class or record that holds a MutableList, a HashMap or an array, then search for its copy( or wither calls. Each may hand out a shared shopping list.

Next, we'll stop building our own objects and start fitting other people's. When an old program speaks a different language from ours, how do we use it without its words spreading through the shop?

sections.h: Named and default arguments replace most builders
sections.html:
Here's how the shop prints a parcel label today:

Java
new Label("12 Mill Lane", "Anna", true, false, true, 2, null);   // which true is fragile?
Kotlin
Label("12 Mill Lane", "Anna", true, false, true, 2, null)         // Kotlin allows the same mess

Seven arguments, three of them true or false, and only their positions say what they mean. Even the author of Label has to count. Java classes like this often grow a telescoping constructor: one constructor per combination of optional parameters, each calling the next with one more default. That's the sandwich ordered in one breath.

The Java fix is the builder from Effective Java (item 2), the best-known book of Java advice: a helper object with one method per field and a build() at the end, as in Label.builder("12 Mill Lane", "Anna").fragile(true).copies(2).build(). It's the sandwich counter. You add one part at a time, and build() hands over the finished object. It works, and it costs a second class that repeats every field.

Kotlin removes most of the problem in the language. Parameters can have defaults, and callers can name them. Here's the label as a data class, a Kotlin class that gets equals, toString and copy for free. Its Java twin is a record, a class that only carries data:

Java
// Java has no named or default arguments: the record keeps the rules, a builder supplies the defaults
record Label(String address, String name, boolean fragile, boolean thisWayUp,
             boolean express, int copies, String note) {
    Label {
        if (copies < 1) throw new IllegalArgumentException("copies must be >= 1");
    }
    Label withExpress(boolean e) {
        return new Label(address, name, fragile, thisWayUp, e, copies, note);
    }
}

var label = Label.builder("12 Mill Lane", "Anna").fragile(true).copies(2).build();   // the builder: next section
var rushed = label.withExpress(true);
Kotlin
data class Label(
    val address: String,
    val name: String,
    val fragile: Boolean = false,
    val thisWayUp: Boolean = false,
    val express: Boolean = false,
    val copies: Int = 1,
    val note: String? = null,
) {
    init { require(copies >= 1) { "copies must be >= 1" } }
}

val label = Label(address = "12 Mill Lane", name = "Anna", fragile = true, copies = 2)
val rushed = label.copy(express = true)

In the Kotlin version, every argument at the call site says what it is. Optional ones can be left out, in any order. copy gives you a changed copy for free (copies get their own section at the end of this lesson). And the init block, which runs whenever an object is constructed, runs for copy too, so nobody can skip the check. That covers what most Java builders do. Named arguments are the sandwich you can order in one breath after all, because each part comes with its name.

Java callers are the gap. Java has no named arguments, so it sees one constructor with seven parameters. @JvmOverloads on the Kotlin constructor generates overloads for Java, one for each trailing default, which is better than nothing and worse than a builder. If Java code will call the class a lot, give it a real builder.

Name the arguments and default the rest. Most builders disappear.

A rule of thumb for porting Java to Kotlin: if every call site of a Java builder sets two or three fields and leaves the rest alone, the Kotlin version is a data class with defaults and nothing else. If call sites build the object across a loop or an if, keep a builder, as the next section explains.

Check yourself. In the Kotlin Label, what does label.copy(copies = 0) do, and why? (It throws IllegalArgumentException. copy builds the new object through the primary constructor, the one in the class header, so the init block runs again.)

Named arguments cover the flat, simple cases. A builder is still the better tool in a few others, and the next section names them.

sections.h: When a builder still earns its place
sections.html:
Builders still win in four cases. The first is Java callers, as we just saw. The second is a check that needs the whole object: "a this-way-up arrow only goes on a fragile label" relates two fields. The third is an object built across several steps, such as notes added in a loop, or a neighbor's name added only when nobody is home. Kotlin's buildList { } and buildString { } are standard-library builders for exactly this. The fourth is nested data, which gets its own section next.

The modern Java shape is a record that checks plus a small builder that only collects. Here's the shop's request to its courier:

Java
record DeliveryRequest(String address, String speed, Map<String, String> notes, Duration window, int retries) {
    DeliveryRequest {                             // compact constructor: runs on every path
        Objects.requireNonNull(address, "address");
        notes = Map.copyOf(notes);                // unmodifiable, and a copy
        if (retries < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("retries must be >= 0");
    }
    DeliveryRequest withWindow(Duration w) { return new DeliveryRequest(address, speed, notes, w, retries); }
    static Builder builder(String address) { return new Builder(address); }
    // Builder: fields with defaults, one setter each, and build() calls the constructor
}
Kotlin
data class DeliveryRequest(
    val address: String,
    val speed: String = "STANDARD",
    val notes: Map<String, String> = emptyMap(),
    val window: Duration = Duration.ofHours(2),
    val retries: Int = 0,
) {
    init { require(retries >= 0) { "retries must be >= 0" } }   // runs on every path, copy() too
}
// no builder and no withers: named arguments and copy(window = ...) do both jobs

retries is how many more times the driver comes back when nobody is home, and window is how long the customer will wait in. The builder holds no rules. The rules live in the record's compact constructor, which build(), the method withWindow and a direct new DeliveryRequest(...) all go through. A compact constructor is a record constructor written without a parameter list. Its body runs first, and Java assigns the fields from the parameters after it, which is why notes = Map.copyOf(notes) changes what gets stored.

A wither is a method like withWindow that returns a copy with one field changed. Java has no with syntax for records yet, so you write one small wither per field you want to change. The Kotlin twin needs neither builder nor withers, and its init block plays the part of the compact constructor.

RecordBuilderDemo, in the Try it, builds one request and pokes at it:

built:        DeliveryRequest[address=12 Mill Lane, speed=EXPRESS, notes={door=blue gate}, window=PT2H, retries=2]
narrower:     PT30M
notes:        unmodifiable
wither:       retries must be >= 0, was -1

The wither couldn't sneak past the check either. The JDK's newer APIs follow the same idea, a builder that produces an object nobody can change: HttpClient.newBuilder(), and Thread.ofVirtual(), which returns a Thread.Builder.

One builder bug deserves a name. If build() checks but the class also has a public constructor that doesn't, half the program skips the rules. That's a sandwich counter with a side door into the kitchen. Put the rules in the type, never only in the builder.

The builders so far make flat things. An order has a list of items inside it and notes beside them, and for nested data Kotlin has a neater tool.

try.title: Find where the rules live
steps: Run RecordBuilderDemo with the command below, and read the four lines.
In the Java main, change .retries(2) to .retries(-1) (in Kotlin, retries = 2 to retries = -1). Predict: which line throws, and from where? Run it.

code.title: RecordBuilderDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l03; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.LinkedHashMap; import java.util.Map; import java.util.Objects; /** A record with a small builder: the record checks, the builder only collects. */ public class RecordBuilderDemo { record DeliveryRequest(String address, String speed, Map<String, String> notes, Duration window, int retries) { DeliveryRequest { // every path to a DeliveryRequest runs this Objects.requireNonNull(address, "address"); notes = Map.copyOf(notes); // really unmodifiable if (retries < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("retries must be >= 0, was " + retries); } DeliveryRequest withWindow(Duration w) { // a hand-written "wither" return new DeliveryRequest(address, speed, notes, w, retries); } DeliveryRequest withRetries(int n) { return new DeliveryRequest(address, speed, notes, window, n); } static Builder builder(String address) { return new Builder(address); } static final class Builder { private final String address; private String speed = "STANDARD"; private final Map<String, String> notes = new LinkedHashMap<>(); private Duration window = Duration.ofHours(2); private int retries = 0; private Builder(String address) { this.address = address; } Builder speed(String s) { speed = s; return this; } Builder note(String k, String v) { notes.put(k, v); return this; } Builder window(Duration w) { window = w; return this; } Builder retries(int n) { retries = n; return this; } DeliveryRequest build() { return new DeliveryRequest(address, speed, notes, window, retries); } } } public static void main(String[] args) { DeliveryRequest req = DeliveryRequest.builder("12 Mill Lane") .speed("EXPRESS") .note("door", "blue gate") .retries(2) .build(); System.out.println("built: " + req); System.out.println("narrower: " + req.withWindow(Duration.ofMinutes(30)).window()); try { req.notes().put("dog", "friendly"); } catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) { System.out.println("notes: unmodifiable"); } try { req.withRetries(-1); // the wither can't skip the check either } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println("wither: " + e.getMessage()); } } }

alt.title: RecordBuilderDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l03 import java.time.Duration // The Kotlin twin of RecordBuilderDemo.java: no builder and no withers, because named arguments, // defaults and copy() do both jobs. The rules still live in one place: init. data class DeliveryRequest( val address: String, val speed: String = "STANDARD", val notes: Map<String, String> = emptyMap(), val window: Duration = Duration.ofHours(2), val retries: Int = 0, ) { init { // runs for every construction, copy() included require(retries >= 0) { "retries must be >= 0, was $retries" } } } fun main() { val req = DeliveryRequest( address = "12 Mill Lane", speed = "EXPRESS", notes = mapOf("door" to "blue gate"), retries = 2, ) println("built: $req") println("narrower: ${req.copy(window = Duration.ofMinutes(30)).window}") // Map is a read-only type, so there is no put(). Force a cast and the map behind it refuses too: val write = runCatching { (req.notes as MutableMap<String, String>)["dog"] = "friendly" } println("notes: ${if (write.isFailure) "unmodifiable" else "writable!"}") try { req.copy(retries = -1) // copy() can't skip the check either } catch (e: IllegalArgumentException) { println("copy(): ${e.message}") } }

try.expect: The first run prints the built request, PT30M for the narrower copy, notes: unmodifiable and wither: retries must be >= 0, was -1. With .retries(-1) the program stops in build() with IllegalArgumentException: retries must be >= 0, was -1, and the stack trace's top line is the record's compact constructor, RecordBuilderDemo$DeliveryRequest.<init>, called from Builder.build. The builder has no rules of its own, so it can't forget any. The Kotlin twin fails in the same place, its init block, and in a normal run prints copy(): retries must be >= 0, was -1.

sections.h: Type-safe builders: lambdas with receivers and @DslMarker
sections.html:
For nested data, Kotlin lets you write a builder that reads like a filled-in form. Here's an order in the lab's DSL, a domain-specific language: a small language for one job, written inside Kotlin.

Java
// Java has no lambdas with receivers; the closest is a Consumer that receives the builder
Order o = order(b -> {
    b.customer("anna@example.com");
    b.items(items -> {
        items.item("rye bread", 450);
        items.item("oat milk", 220);
    });
    b.note("door", "blue gate");
});
Kotlin
val o = order {
    customer = "anna@example.com"
    items {
        item("rye bread", 450)
        item("oat milk", 220)
    }
    note("door", "blue gate")
}

That's the sandwich counter again, with a smaller counter inside it for the items. The trick is a lambda with receiver. order takes an OrderBuilder.() -> Unit: a function that runs with a builder as this. Inside the braces, customer and items are members of that builder, so you call them with no prefix:

Java
static Order order(Consumer<OrderBuilder> block) {
    OrderBuilder b = new OrderBuilder();
    block.accept(b);                                   // the block gets the builder as a parameter
    return b.build();
}

final class OrderBuilder {
    private String customer;
    private final List<Item> items = new ArrayList<>();
    void customer(String c) { customer = c; }
    void items(Consumer<ItemsBuilder> block) {
        ItemsBuilder b = new ItemsBuilder();
        block.accept(b);
        items.addAll(b.build());
    }
    Order build() { /* check, then copy into the order */ }
}
Kotlin
fun order(block: OrderBuilder.() -> Unit): Order =
    OrderBuilder().apply(block).build()

class OrderBuilder {
    var customer: String? = null
    private val items = mutableListOf<Item>()
    fun items(block: ItemsBuilder.() -> Unit) { items += ItemsBuilder().apply(block).build() }
    fun build(): Order { /* check, then copy into the order */ }
}

Read OrderBuilder().apply(block) as "make a builder, run the block with it as this, and hand the builder back". Gradle's Kotlin build files (the files that build this course's labs) and the kotlinx.html library, for writing web pages in Kotlin, are built the same way. The builder is still a builder: build() is the one place that sees every field, so it checks them there.

There's one trap. Inside items { }, two receivers, objects that this can refer to, are in scope: the ItemsBuilder and the outer OrderBuilder. So customer = "x" written inside the inner block compiles, and quietly sets the outer field. The demo in the Try it shows this on a delivery round, a driver and a list of stops. Without protection, one innocent-looking line inside the stops block changed the driver:

Round(driver=oops, stops=[Stop(orderId=o-101, parcels=2), Stop(orderId=o-102, parcels=3)])

@DslMarker closes that hole. It's an annotation for annotations: you mark your own annotation with it, then put yours on every builder class.

Java
// Java needs no marker: each block names its builder, so reaching the outer one means typing b
b.items(items -> {
    items.item("rye bread", 450);
    b.customer("x");       // compiles, but you can see it in review
});
Kotlin
@DslMarker annotation class OrderDsl

@OrderDsl class OrderBuilder { ... }
@OrderDsl class ItemsBuilder { ... }

With both builders marked, the compiler only lets you call members of the nearest receiver without a prefix. Reaching the outer one needs an explicit label, this@order.customer, which nobody writes by accident.

Mark every builder in a DSL. Then an inner block can't reach outside by accident.

Build a DSL only when the data nests. A flat label with seven fields is clearer with named arguments, and a DSL would add two classes for nothing. The payoff comes with structure, like items inside an order or stops on a delivery round. It also helps when many people write the same kind of thing, because inside each block the editor offers only that builder's methods.

Building is half of this lesson. The other half starts from an object you already have.

try.title: Make the inner block reach outside
steps: Uncomment the line driver = "oops" inside the stops { } block. Predict, then run.
Now delete both @RoundDsl lines above the two builder classes (keep the annotation class itself) and run again. Who is driving the round now?
Restore the file. Then open the Java twin and uncomment rb.driver("oops"): it compiles, but notice that you had to type the outer builder's name.

code.title: DslScope.kt
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l03 // A tiny delivery-round DSL. @DslMarker stops an inner block from reaching the outer builder by accident. @DslMarker annotation class RoundDsl data class Stop(val orderId: String, val parcels: Int) data class Round(val driver: String, val stops: List<Stop>) @RoundDsl class StopsBuilder { private val stops = mutableListOf<Stop>() fun stop(orderId: String, parcels: Int) { stops += Stop(orderId, parcels) } fun build() = stops.toList() } @RoundDsl class RoundBuilder { var driver: String = "unassigned" private var stops: List<Stop> = emptyList() fun stops(block: StopsBuilder.() -> Unit) { stops = StopsBuilder().apply(block).build() } fun build() = Round(driver, stops) } fun round(block: RoundBuilder.() -> Unit): Round = RoundBuilder().apply(block).build() fun main() { val r = round { driver = "Sam" stops { stop("o-101", 2) stop("o-102", 3) // driver = "oops" // step 2 of the Try it: uncomment this line } } println(r) println("parcels on the van: ${r.stops.sumOf { it.parcels }}") }

alt.title: DslScopeJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l03; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.function.Consumer; /** * The Java twin of DslScope.kt. Java has no lambdas with receivers, so each block is a Consumer * that gets its builder as a named parameter. */ public class DslScopeJava { record Stop(String orderId, int parcels) {} record Round(String driver, List<Stop> stops) {} static final class StopsBuilder { private final List<Stop> stops = new ArrayList<>(); StopsBuilder stop(String orderId, int parcels) { stops.add(new Stop(orderId, parcels)); return this; } List<Stop> build() { return List.copyOf(stops); } } static final class RoundBuilder { private String driver = "unassigned"; private List<Stop> stops = List.of(); RoundBuilder driver(String d) { driver = d; return this; } RoundBuilder stops(Consumer<StopsBuilder> block) { StopsBuilder b = new StopsBuilder(); block.accept(b); stops = b.build(); return this; } Round build() { return new Round(driver, stops); } } static Round round(Consumer<RoundBuilder> block) { RoundBuilder b = new RoundBuilder(); block.accept(b); return b.build(); } public static void main(String[] args) { Round r = round(rb -> { rb.driver("Sam"); rb.stops(s -> { s.stop("o-101", 2); s.stop("o-102", 3); // rb.driver("oops"); // step 4 of the Try it: this compiles, but you have to name rb }); }); System.out.println(r); System.out.println("parcels on the van: " + r.stops().stream().mapToInt(Stop::parcels).sum()); } }

try.expect: The first run prints a round with driver=Sam and parcels on the van: 5. With the line uncommented, the build fails: 'var driver: String' cannot be called in this context with an implicit receiver. Use an explicit receiver if necessary. Without the marker it compiles and prints driver=oops: the inner block quietly rewrote the outer round. The Java twin prints driver=oops too, but the line that did it says rb. in plain sight.

sections.h: Prototype: every copy is shallow until you make it safe
sections.html:
Now the photocopier. Prototype means making a new object by copying an existing one and changing a few fields. The shop does this every week: the Saturday breakfast box is set up once, and each customer gets a copy with their own name and notes. Tests do it too, with one sample order copied and changed in each test.

Java's original tool for this, Cloneable, is broken by design. The interface has no clone method, so implementing it gives callers nothing to call. Object.clone() is protected, and it makes a shallow copy (more on that in a moment). To use it, you override clone, call super.clone(), catch a CloneNotSupportedException that can't happen, and then fix every changeable field by hand. Skip it. Use a copy constructor, a static copy factory, or a wither on a record.

Records make withers easy to write, and Kotlin data classes generate copy(). Neither copies deeply. The Kotlin docs say it plainly: copy() creates a shallow copy, and references to other objects are shared. A shallow copy copies each field's value, and when the value is a reference to another object, such as a list, it copies the reference, not the list:

Java
record Cart(String id, List<String> items) {
    Cart withId(String newId) { return new Cart(newId, items); }   // a wither: shares the list
}
var c1 = new Cart("c1", new ArrayList<>(List.of("bread")));
var c2 = c1.withId("c2");
c2.items().add("milk");     // c1.items() is now [bread, milk]
Kotlin
data class Cart(val id: String, val items: MutableList<String>)
val c1 = Cart("c1", mutableListOf("bread"))
val c2 = c1.copy(id = "c2")
c2.items += "milk"          // c1.items is now [bread, milk]

That was the warm-up. copy() is very obliging: it copies exactly what you asked for, the reference, and not one thing more. Here the photocopier picture breaks. A photocopy is a separate piece of paper, and writing on it never changes the original. But picture a form with a shopping list clipped to it. copy() gives you a new form with the same shopping list clipped on, so writing on the copy's list writes on the original's. The figure shows both carts holding one list.

The fix is the same in both languages. Store collections that can't change, List.copyOf in a compact constructor in Java and a read-only List in Kotlin, and let withers build a new collection: copy(items = items + "milk"). Then sharing is harmless, because nobody can write on the shared sheet.

A copy is only as safe as the parts it shares. Share only parts that can't change.

Kotlin has a second trap. data class Email private constructor(val value: String) still gets a public copy(), so Email.of("anna@example.com").copy(value = "not-an-email") compiles and skips your factory. Kotlin 2.4 only warns, at the line that calls copy:

w: CopyTrap.kt:29:24 This 'copy()' exposes the non-public primary constructor of a 'data class'. ... This will become an error in language version 2.5.

Add @ConsistentCopyVisibility to make copy() as private as the constructor today. A check in an init block is safer still, because copy() runs it. Java records never had this illusion. A record's canonical constructor, the one that takes every component, can't be less visible than the record itself, so the rules belong in the compact constructor from the start.

Check yourself. The shop's breakfast box template is a data class with val tags: MutableList<String>. Anna's copy gets the tag "no nuts" through annasBox.tags += "no nuts". What do Ben's box and the template now say? (Both say no nuts too, because all three share one list. With a read-only List and copy(tags = tags + "no nuts"), only Anna's box changes.)

try.title: Trigger both copy traps
steps: Read CopyTrap.kt (or its Java twin) and predict the three lines it prints.
Run it. If Gradle compiles the file again, read the w: warnings too.
Add @ConsistentCopyVisibility on the line above data class Email, and run again.

code.title: CopyTrap.kt
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l03 // Two traps in data class copy(): it is shallow, and it ignores a private constructor. data class Cart(val id: String, val items: MutableList<String>) data class Email private constructor(val value: String) { companion object { fun of(raw: String): Email { require("@" in raw) { "not an email: $raw" } return Email(raw) } } } data class Price(val cents: Long) { init { require(cents >= 0) { "negative price: $cents" } } } fun main() { // trap 1: copy() copies the reference to the list, not the list val c1 = Cart("c1", mutableListOf("bread")) val c2 = c1.copy(id = "c2") c2.items += "milk" println("c1.items after changing c2: ${c1.items}") // trap 2: the private constructor does not cover the generated copy() val email = Email.of("anna@example.com") val broken = email.copy(value = "not-an-email") println("copy() skipped the factory: $broken") // init blocks DO run on copy() val result = runCatching { Price(5).copy(cents = -1) } println("Price(5).copy(cents = -1): ${result.exceptionOrNull()?.message}") }

alt.title: CopyTrapJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l03; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** The Java twin of CopyTrap.kt: record copies are shallow, and a factory can't hide a record's constructor. */ public class CopyTrapJava { record Cart(String id, List<String> items) { Cart withId(String newId) { return new Cart(newId, items); } // a hand-written wither: shares the list } record Email(String value) { // a record's canonical constructor is never more private than the record itself, // so this factory can always be bypassed with new Email(...) static Email of(String raw) { if (!raw.contains("@")) throw new IllegalArgumentException("not an email: " + raw); return new Email(raw); } } record Price(long cents) { Price { // compact constructor: every path runs it if (cents < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative price: " + cents); } Price withCents(long c) { return new Price(c); } } public static void main(String[] args) { // trap 1: the wither copies the reference to the list, not the list Cart c1 = new Cart("c1", new ArrayList<>(List.of("bread"))); Cart c2 = c1.withId("c2"); c2.items().add("milk"); System.out.println("c1.items after changing c2: " + c1.items()); // trap 2: the factory checks, the canonical constructor doesn't Email broken = new Email("not-an-email"); System.out.println("new skipped the factory: " + broken); // the compact constructor DOES run on withers try { new Price(5).withCents(-1); } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println("new Price(5).withCents(-1): " + e.getMessage()); } } }

try.expect: It prints c1.items after changing c2: [bread, milk] (the copy shared the list), copy() skipped the factory: Email(value=not-an-email), and Price(5).copy(cents = -1): negative price: -1, because init runs on copy(). The compiler warns twice: Non-public primary constructor is exposed via the generated 'copy()' method of the 'data' class. on the class, and a second warning at the copy call that says it will become an error in language version 2.5. With @ConsistentCopyVisibility, the build stops with Cannot access 'fun copy(value: String = ...): Email': it is private in 'workbench.patterns.l03.Email'. The Java twin tells the same story: the wither shares the list, new Email("not-an-email") skips the factory, and the compact constructor rejects -1.

video.title: A copy copies the arrow, not the object: two carts share one list until the list can't change and a change builds a new one; named and default arguments replace most builders

compare.title: A prototype that copies safely

java.title: DeliveryPlan.java
java.html: record DeliveryPlan(String district, List<String> days, Map<String, Long> feeCents) { DeliveryPlan { // every copy passes through here days = List.copyOf(days); feeCents = Map.copyOf(feeCents); } DeliveryPlan forDistrict(String d) { // safe to share: nothing can change return new DeliveryPlan(d, days, feeCents); } DeliveryPlan withDay(String day) { // copy, change the copy, wrap again var copy = new ArrayList<>(days); copy.add(day); return new DeliveryPlan(district, copy, feeCents); } } var base = new DeliveryPlan("town center", List.of("MON", "THU"), Map.of("BIKE", 250L)); var harbour = base.forDistrict("harbour").withDay("SAT");

kotlin.title: DeliveryPlan.kt
kotlin.html: data class DeliveryPlan( val district: String, val days: List<String>, // read-only types val feeCents: Map<String, Long>, ) val base = DeliveryPlan("town center", listOf("MON", "THU"), mapOf("BIKE" to 250L)) val harbour = base.copy( district = "harbour", days = base.days + "SAT", // + builds a new list )

compare.note: Kotlin generates copy() with named arguments, so it needs no withers, and + on a read-only List or Map returns a new collection. Java needs one hand-written wither per field. Both copies are shallow, and the safety comes from the parts, not from the copy. There's one real difference. Java's compact constructor can replace the incoming list with List.copyOf, while a Kotlin data class property can't be reassigned in init. A Kotlin List parameter is only read-only, so a caller who passes a MutableList and keeps a reference to it can still change it. If that matters, take the list as a plain constructor parameter and store toList() in a property.

worked.title: From a telescoping constructor to a record and builder, and to a Kotlin class

steps.say: Here's the label call from the first section, with all seven arguments. Before reading on, say which argument is the note, and which rules you'd expect Label to enforce.
steps.code: new Label("12 Mill Lane", "Anna", true, true, false, 1, "ring twice");

alt.html: Label("12 Mill Lane", "Anna", true, true, false, 1, "ring twice")

steps.say: Put every rule in one place that all paths go through: the record's compact constructor in Java, the init block in Kotlin. The rule that relates two fields (a this-way-up arrow only goes on a fragile label) can only be checked where all the fields are known. Kotlin also gets its defaults here, which is half of what a builder does.
steps.code: record Label(String address, String name, boolean fragile, boolean thisWayUp, boolean express, int copies, String note) { Label { if (copies < 1) throw new IllegalArgumentException("copies must be >= 1"); // 1. one-field rules if (note != null && note.length() > 30) throw new IllegalArgumentException("note is too long"); if (thisWayUp && !fragile) // 2. a rule across fields throw new IllegalArgumentException("this-way-up arrows only go on fragile labels"); } }

alt.html: data class Label @JvmOverloads constructor( val address: String, val name: String, val fragile: Boolean = false, // 3. defaults live in the signature val thisWayUp: Boolean = false, val express: Boolean = false, val copies: Int = 1, val note: String? = null, ) { init { require(copies >= 1) { "copies must be >= 1" } // 1. one-field rules require(note == null || note.length <= 30) { "note is too long" } require(!thisWayUp || fragile) { // 2. a rule across fields "this-way-up arrows only go on fragile labels" } } }

steps.say: Java needs a builder that only collects and supplies defaults. Its build() calls the record's constructor, so the rules run there. Kotlin needs no builder: named arguments do the job, and @JvmOverloads gives Java callers some overloads. If Java code calls the Kotlin class often, add a builder for it too.
steps.code: // inside record Label static Builder builder(String address, String name) { return new Builder(address, name); } static final class Builder { private final String address; private final String name; private boolean fragile, thisWayUp, express; private int copies = 1; private String note; // 3. defaults Builder(String address, String name) { this.address = address; this.name = name; } // 4. required up front Builder fragile(boolean f) { fragile = f; return this; } Builder thisWayUp(boolean t) { thisWayUp = t; return this; } Builder copies(int n) { copies = n; return this; } Builder note(String n) { note = n; return this; } Label build() { return new Label(address, name, fragile, thisWayUp, express, copies, note); } } var label = Label.builder("12 Mill Lane", "Anna").fragile(true).thisWayUp(true).note("ring twice").build();

alt.html: // 4. required values have no default, so the compiler insists on them val label = Label("12 Mill Lane", "Anna", fragile = true, thisWayUp = true, note = "ring twice") val rushed = label.copy(express = true) // the "wither" is generated

lab.title: A checking order DSL, and a prototype that stops leaking
steps: Open the two files. OrderDsl.kt is the order DSL from this lesson, and OrderTemplate is the shop's prototype for regular orders such as the Saturday breakfast box.
Run the tests. Twelve of thirteen fail: the DSL is all TODO, and OrderTemplate leaks tags and notes between copies.
In OrderDsl.kt, write ItemsBuilder: keep a private MutableList, and return toList() from build().

Write OrderBuilder: items runs the block on a fresh ItemsBuilder and keeps its items, note puts into a private map, and build() checks with require and copies the collections into the Order. Then write order. Put @OrderDsl on both builder classes.
Fix OrderTemplate.java: add a compact constructor that stores List.copyOf and Map.copyOf, and make the withers copy the collection, change the copy, and build a new template.
Run the tests until all thirteen pass.
hints: require(condition) { "customer is required" } throws IllegalArgumentException with that message when the condition is false.
ItemsBuilder().apply(block).build(): apply runs the lambda with the builder as this and returns the builder.
In a record's compact constructor, tags = List.copyOf(tags); replaces the parameter before the field is set. You don't write this.tags = ....
lab.done: All thirteen tests in OrderDslTest and OrderTemplateTest pass.

drill.title: A two-level DSL from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write fun round(block: RoundBuilder.() -> Unit): Round, where the builder has a var driver and a nested stops { stop(orderId, parcels) } block, and @DslMarker stops the inner block from setting driver. Then compare with the answer, and with the Java twin built from Consumers.

answer.html: @DslMarker annotation class RoundDsl data class Stop(val orderId: String, val parcels: Int) data class Round(val driver: String, val stops: List<Stop>) @RoundDsl class StopsBuilder { private val stops = mutableListOf<Stop>() fun stop(orderId: String, parcels: Int) { stops += Stop(orderId, parcels) } fun build() = stops.toList() } @RoundDsl class RoundBuilder { var driver: String = "unassigned" private var stops: List<Stop> = emptyList() fun stops(block: StopsBuilder.() -> Unit) { stops = StopsBuilder().apply(block).build() } fun build() = Round(driver, stops) } fun round(block: RoundBuilder.() -> Unit): Round = RoundBuilder().apply(block).build()

alt.title: Java
alt.html: // Java has no lambdas with receivers: each block is a Consumer of its builder record Stop(String orderId, int parcels) {} record Round(String driver, List<Stop> stops) {} final class StopsBuilder { private final List<Stop> stops = new ArrayList<>(); void stop(String orderId, int parcels) { stops.add(new Stop(orderId, parcels)); } List<Stop> build() { return List.copyOf(stops); } } final class RoundBuilder { private String driver = "unassigned"; private List<Stop> stops = List.of(); void driver(String d) { driver = d; } void stops(Consumer<StopsBuilder> block) { StopsBuilder b = new StopsBuilder(); block.accept(b); stops = b.build(); } Round build() { return new Round(driver, stops); } } static Round round(Consumer<RoundBuilder> block) { RoundBuilder b = new RoundBuilder(); block.accept(b); return b.build(); }

recap: Kotlin's named and default arguments, plus copy(), replace most builders. Put the checks in init: it runs for every construction, copy() included.
A builder still helps for Java callers, for objects built over several steps, and for nested data. In Java, pair a checking record (its compact constructor) with a builder that only collects.
A type-safe DSL is a function that takes a lambda with receiver (Builder.() -> Unit). @DslMarker stops an inner block from quietly reaching an outer builder.
Cloneable has no clone method, and Object.clone() is shallow. Use copy constructors, copy factories or withers.
Record withers and data class copy() are shallow. Store collections that can't change, and build new collections in withers.

The limit: no copy in either language is deep, so a copy is only as safe as the parts it shares. And in Kotlin 2.4, a private constructor doesn't make copy() private without @ConsistentCopyVisibility.

explain.prompt: A colleague says: "Kotlin data classes can't change, so copy() gives us safe, independent order templates." Explain where that's wrong, and how you'd make templates safe in Kotlin and in Java.
explain.answer: A data class is only as unchangeable as its properties. val stops a property from pointing somewhere else, but if it holds a MutableList or a HashMap, copy() copies the reference, so the template and every copy share that collection, and changing one changes all of them. To make templates safe, give them collections that can't change. In Kotlin, use read-only List and Map types, and copy(tags = tags + x) to build new ones. In Java, use a record whose compact constructor stores List.copyOf and Map.copyOf, and withers that copy, change the copy and construct a new record. I'd also put the rules in init or the compact constructor, because copy() and withers go through them.

deeper.html:
Effective Java's hierarchical builder solves a problem you may meet in a shared Java library: a Pizza.Builder that subclasses (NyPizza.Builder, Calzone.Builder) extend without losing the subclass's type in a chain of calls. It uses a recursive type parameter, Builder<T extends Builder<T>>, and an abstract self() method that each subclass implements as return this;. Advanced generics: recursive bounds, T & Any, @UnsafeVariance in the generics track showed why that recursive bound works. In Kotlin you almost never need it, because named arguments and copy() remove the chain.

Java has no with syntax for records yet. Project Amber, the OpenJDK project for smaller language features, has proposed one, derived record creation (JEP 468), where you would write something like point with { x = 3; }. Check its status on the JEP page before you plan around it. Until then, write withers for the fields that really change.

People sometimes copy a whole tree of objects deeply by turning it into bytes and back (serialization), or with a reflection library. It works, it's slow, and it copies things you didn't mean to copy, such as a shared clock or an open connection. If you need a deep copy, the cleaner fix is usually to make the parts unchangeable, so a shallow copy is enough.

Kotlin's buildList { add(...) }, buildMap { } and buildString { } are small standard-library builders with receivers. Use them when you build a collection with loops or conditions; the result is read-only once the block returns.
